issue.title: refactor: redesign observability with Sentry error reporting and OTel traces
issue.body:
## Problem Statement

The current observability system is present but not reliably actionable. Operators can see that an MCP session, tool, or process failed, but often cannot determine why, which release introduced the problem, which MCP client experienced it, or whether multiple events represent the same underlying failure.

The current design also spreads telemetry policy across the Node entrypoint, tool observer, SDK observer, API observer, core observation types, tests, and documentation. Each new diagnostic field requires more manual allowlisting and more privacy regression tests. That has created a choice between exporting opaque errors and exporting native exceptions with an unacceptable risk of leaking user data.

Issue #915 documented a concrete example: hundreds of process-failure traces were grouped under generic `McpProcessFailure`/`Error` fields without enough information to distinguish runtime, transport, SDK, and application failures. PR #920 explored moving more of the privacy decision into the Collector, but it changes the data policy before the desired observability contract and introduces raw exception plumbing into the runtime-neutral core.

The current error destination is a self-hosted GlitchTip project. We want to return to Sentry as the error-reporting backend, with proper release tracking, issue grouping, source maps, alerts, and trace correlation. GlitchTip should be removed from the active configuration and documentation.

### Goals

- Make user-visible failures actionable in Sentry.
- Make OTel traces explain what happened before and during a failure.
- Preserve low-cardinality metrics for reliability and performance dashboards.
- Capture sanitized exception messages and stacks without exporting prompts, tool arguments, tool results, credentials, or fitness data.
- Report each logical failure once instead of duplicating it across nested spans and SDK hooks.
- Keep the core package runtime-neutral and free of native exception transport concerns.
- Make the telemetry implementation easier to change by concentrating policy behind a small, deep Node adapter.
- Migrate error reporting from GlitchTip to Sentry SaaS without losing release/source-map diagnostics.

## Solution

Adopt a deliberate two-backend model:

- **Sentry** is the source of truth for actionable errors, crashes, releases, issue grouping, source maps, and error alerts.
- **OpenTelemetry through the Collector to Honeycomb** is the source of truth for traces, latency, retries, sessions, and aggregate metrics.
- **The Collector** performs tail sampling, routing, retention, and final defense-in-depth scrubbing. It is not the only privacy policy enforcement point.

Sentry performance tracing remains disabled. OTel traces remain independent from Sentry, with OTel trace and span identifiers attached to Sentry error events for navigation between systems.

### Failure reporter seam

Introduce one deep Node-only failure-reporting module with a small interface. Callers provide the native error and structured failure context; the module returns an optional correlation/event receipt.

The module will:

1. Classify known error types such as Hevy HTTP, network, validation, protocol, SDK, lifecycle, and process failures.
2. Produce one stable failure record containing bounded taxonomy and operational context.
3. Sanitize the message and stack once, with length, line, path, credential, URL, and nested-cause limits.
4. Send one sanitized exception to Sentry.
5. Attach the same structured fields and a standard exception event to the owning OTel span.
6. Link the Sentry event to the active OTel trace and expose a short diagnostic/correlation ID where appropriate.
7. Treat telemetry failures as best-effort and never alter MCP behavior.

The runtime-neutral core will retain only safe observation data. Native `unknown` exceptions will not be added to the core observation contract. The Node observer already wraps execution and can retain the native error at the Node seam.

### Approved diagnostic data

Capture as structured context:

- service, release, runtime, OS, and architecture;
- MCP transport and sanitized client/protocol metadata;
- fixed tool name, feature, operation, and read/write kind;
- API method, normalized endpoint, status, retry count, timeout phase, and commit state;
- stable error type, category, code, expectedness, and retryability;
- bounded sanitized message and stack for actionable failures;
- OTel trace/span IDs, Sentry event ID, and a per-failure diagnostic ID.

Never capture:

- API keys, bearer tokens, authorization headers, or request bodies;
- prompts, prompt arguments, tool arguments, or tool result text;
- raw Hevy identifiers, exact dates, workout/routine/template content, names, notes, or measurements;
- arbitrary error object properties, complete response bodies, or URLs containing query data;
- a persistent identity derived from the Hevy API key.

Telemetry is enabled by default for the packaged Node runtime. `HEVY_MCP_TELEMETRY=0` disables all project telemetry. Add a separate diagnostic-detail opt-out so users can retain structural metrics/traces while suppressing exception messages and stacks.

### Error ownership

Define one owner for each logical failure:

- Tool exceptions are captured by the Node tool observer.
- API observers supply structured API context; the tool-level reporter owns the user-visible exception.
- Returned MCP errors affect span status and metrics but do not create exception events.
- Expected not-found outcomes affect metrics and traces but do not create Sentry issues.
- SDK/protocol failures are captured by the SDK adapter.
- Startup and process failures are captured once by the lifecycle/process adapter.
- Telemetry exporter failures are not reported as application failures.

Nested spans may still receive status and bounded attributes, but the native exception is recorded only on the owning span.

### Sentry migration

Move the default error destination from GlitchTip to Sentry SaaS:

- Provision/configure the Sentry project, environments, ownership, retention, and alerts.
- Use a packaged public Sentry DSN with a runtime `SENTRY_DSN` override; an empty value disables Sentry export.
- Continue using the Sentry organization, project, and auth token in release CI for private source-map upload.
- Configure explicit Sentry integrations so automatic process handlers do not duplicate the custom failure reporter.
- Use `captureException` once per logical failure rather than generic exception messages for actionable errors.
- Add a centralized `beforeSend` final scrubber.
- Set release, environment, stable fingerprints, bounded tags/contexts, and OTel trace correlation.
- Generate source maps during release builds, upload them privately to Sentry, and keep them out of the published package.
- Remove active GlitchTip configuration, documentation, tests, and default DSN references. Historical changelog entries may remain as historical records.
- Audit and remove the direct Sentry OTel integration dependency if it is no longer needed after the independent OTel design is complete.

### OTel and Collector behavior

Keep OTel responsible for traces and metrics:

- Preserve a clear session/request → MCP tool → Hevy API → retry/cache span hierarchy.
- Use standard span status and exception semantics with the sanitized failure record.
- Keep messages and stacks out of metric attributes.
- Retain all error and slow traces at the Collector, and sample successful traces.
- Keep all low-cardinality metrics, with alerts for exporter drops, stale data, queue pressure, and Collector health.
- Maintain a final Collector scrubber and regression fixtures, but do not rely on the Collector as the sole privacy control.

### Worker alignment

The Worker must not import Node telemetry. After the Node design is proven, add a separate Worker adapter that emits the same failure taxonomy and correlation fields through the Worker’s supported logging/error facilities. A Worker-side OTel SDK is not part of the first implementation slice.

## Commits

Each commit below must leave the repository buildable and tests runnable. Runtime/package commits require the appropriate non-empty Changeset before committing, and the Changeset status check must pass before each commit that is prepared for review.

1. **`docs: define observability goals and data contract`**
   - Record the two-backend responsibility split, approved diagnostic fields, prohibited data, retention assumptions, and the Sentry migration decision.
   - Define the failure taxonomy, expected-error policy, and ownership matrix.

2. **`test: add representative failure and redaction fixtures`**
   - Add fixtures for Hevy HTTP errors, network errors, validation errors, SDK errors, process failures, malformed thrown values, nested causes, credentials, local paths, and response-body sentinels.
   - Establish tests against externally visible normalized records rather than private helper implementation details.

3. **`refactor: introduce the centralized failure record normalizer`**
   - Implement the single classifier/scrubber that produces bounded operational fields and sanitized diagnostic details.
   - Keep native error objects inside the Node package.
   - Verify stable behavior for expected errors and unknown thrown values.

4. **`refactor: add the Node failure reporter seam`**
   - Add the small reporter interface and adapters for Sentry and OTel.
   - Add correlation/event receipt handling.
   - Preserve best-effort behavior and make provider failures invisible to MCP callers.

5. **`refactor: route lifecycle and process failures through the reporter`**
   - Replace scattered lifecycle exception attribute construction with structured failure contexts.
   - Ensure startup, connect, runtime, uncaught-exception, and unhandled-rejection failures are captured once.
   - Preserve Node’s normal termination semantics.

6. **`refactor: route tool failures through one owner`**
   - Let the Node tool observer retain and report native tool exceptions at its execution seam.
   - Keep the core completion observation safe and runtime-neutral.
   - Stop the SDK wrapper and nested spans from emitting duplicate native exception events.

7. **`refactor: remove obsolete raw-exception plumbing and duplicated policy`**
   - Remove the proposed native exception field from the core observation contract if present.
   - Delete per-call privacy allowlist spreading and obsolete generic exception adapters.
   - Keep only one source of truth for failure context construction.

8. **`feat: restore Sentry SaaS as the error backend`**
   - Replace the GlitchTip default destination with the packaged Sentry DSN and runtime override behavior.
   - Configure explicit integrations, release/environment metadata, stable fingerprints, `beforeSend` scrubbing, and OTel trace correlation.
   - Update provider mocks and tests for one-event capture and duplicate-handler prevention.

9. **`build: upload private Sentry release artifacts`**
   - Make release builds generate and upload source maps to Sentry without including them in the npm package.
   - Add a release smoke test that verifies readable mapped stack frames and release attribution.

10. **`feat: align OTel span exception and sampling behavior`**
    - Record sanitized standard exception events only on owning spans.
    - Normalize span names and semantic attributes.
    - Add slow/error trace sampling rules and preserve all low-cardinality metrics.

11. **`chore: remove GlitchTip configuration and documentation`**
    - Remove active GlitchTip references, default DSN fixtures, destination assumptions, and obsolete environment descriptions.
    - Leave historical changelog records untouched.
    - Audit dependencies and remove direct packages that are no longer used.

12. **`feat: add observability dashboards and incident runbook`**
    - Migrate error views and alerts from GlitchTip to Sentry.
    - Add release, tool, client, API-status, startup, latency, and trace-correlation views.
    - Document the operator workflow from a Sentry issue to its Honeycomb trace.

13. **`test: verify end-to-end telemetry payloads`**
    - Exercise the actual Sentry event normalization hook and serialized OTel exporter payloads.
    - Verify secret/path/body/prompt absence, one-event ownership, release metadata, source-map attribution, Collector redaction, and exporter-failure resilience.

14. **`feat: align Worker failure diagnostics`**
    - Implement the same stable taxonomy and bounded correlation fields using Worker-supported facilities.
    - Keep this adapter independent from Node packages and defer Worker OTel SDK adoption unless a separate decision approves it.

15. **`refactor: remove superseded telemetry implementation`**
    - Delete dead helpers, stale tests, obsolete documentation, and compatibility paths only after the new behavior has been observed in a controlled release.

## Decision Document

- Sentry SaaS is the error-reporting backend. GlitchTip is removed from active runtime configuration.
- Honeycomb through the OTel Collector remains the trace and metric backend.
- Sentry performance tracing is disabled; OTel tracing is independent.
- Sentry receives one sanitized exception per logical actionable failure.
- OTel receives one sanitized exception event on the owning span plus structured span status/attributes.
- The Collector is a final safety and routing layer, not the only privacy enforcement layer.
- Error messages and stacks are allowed only after centralized bounded scrubbing.
- Prompts, arguments, results, credentials, raw IDs, exact dates, response bodies, and arbitrary object fields remain prohibited.
- No API-key-derived user hash or persistent user behavior identity is introduced.
- A per-failure diagnostic/correlation ID is preferred over persistent user tracking.
- The Node core interface remains runtime-neutral and does not transport native exceptions.
- Sentry’s automatic process-level handlers must not compete with the custom failure reporter.
- Expected not-found and ordinary user/configuration failures should not create noisy Sentry issues; they remain queryable through OTel metrics and traces.
- Public Sentry DSN configuration may be packaged; Sentry auth tokens and release credentials remain CI secrets.
- Source maps are uploaded privately to Sentry and excluded from the public package.
- The first implementation focuses on Node. Worker parity follows after the Node contract is validated.

## Testing Decisions

Good tests will verify externally visible telemetry behavior: what is sent, where it is sent, how it is grouped, whether it correlates to a trace, and whether MCP behavior remains unchanged. Tests should not assert incidental helper structure or the exact number of internal function calls unless that number is part of the duplicate-event contract.

Test coverage will include:

- deterministic normalization of each known error family;
- bounded messages, stacks, causes, paths, codes, statuses, and endpoints;
- removal of credentials, headers, prompts, arguments, results, bodies, and raw identifiers;
- expected-error suppression from Sentry;
- one logical failure producing one Sentry event and one owning OTel exception event;
- OTel trace/span ID and Sentry event ID correlation;
- explicit Sentry integration configuration and absence of duplicate process handlers;
- Sentry release/environment/fingerprint behavior;
- private source-map upload and mapped release stacks;
- actual serialized OTLP spans rather than only mocked `recordException` calls;
- Collector redaction and tail-sampling fixtures;
- provider/network failures not affecting MCP responses, process termination, or shutdown;
- telemetry opt-out and diagnostic-detail opt-out behavior;
- Node/Worker package boundary rules;
- dashboard query smoke checks and telemetry freshness.

Validation for the implementation will include the repository build, formatting/lint checks, type checks, unit tests, focused Node stdio observability tests, release-build tests, and the required Changeset status check.

## Out of Scope

- Exporting raw prompts, tool arguments, tool results, API keys, authorization headers, full request/response bodies, or raw fitness data.
- Adding persistent user-level behavior tracking or deriving a user identity from the Hevy API key.
- Migrating Honeycomb, ClickHouse, or the OTel Collector to another vendor.
- Enabling Sentry performance tracing or adding a Sentry span processor to the OTel provider.
- Adding a Worker-side OTel SDK in the initial Node migration.
- Changing MCP response contracts or exposing internal stack traces to MCP clients.
- Rewriting historical changelog entries that mention GlitchTip.
- Building a general-purpose logging framework.

## Further Notes

- This issue supersedes the narrow diagnostic approach in #915 and should be treated as the architectural follow-up to PR #920.
- Before implementation begins, operators should inspect a representative sample of current Sentry/GlitchTip events and OTel traces, including the 578 process failures referenced by #915, to establish a baseline for noise, duplication, and missing context.
- Success means an operator can open a Sentry issue and answer: which release failed, which MCP client and tool were involved, what stable error/API condition occurred, whether the issue is new or regressed, and which Honeycomb trace shows the failure path.
- The migration should be released in a controlled canary first. Compare event volume, duplicate rate, mapped-stack coverage, trace correlation, and sensitive-field regression results before removing the old compatibility paths.

issue.title: Consolidate Node lifecycle and bound HTTP session capacity
issue.body:
## Outcome

Node stdio and HTTP share one startup/config/telemetry/shutdown lifecycle while HTTP sessions and initialization consume bounded, observable capacity.

## Ownership seam

The Node runtime owns process lifecycle, stdio/HTTP adapters, admission, session state, telemetry providers, and shutdown. Shared operation/outcome behavior stays below it.

## Scope

- Remove duplicated startup paths for config, telemetry, key validation, update checks, failure recording, and shutdown.
- Add session caps, idle expiry, initialization concurrency limits, application body deadlines, and deterministic cleanup.
- Return stable 429/503 recovery guidance for local capacity rejection.
- Cancel active upstream work on disconnect, eviction, and shutdown.
- Contain optional telemetry initialization/export failures so they cannot prevent serving.

## Non-goals

- Merging Node and Worker transports.
- Adding process restart supervision inside the library.
- Weakening host, bearer, body, or session security checks.
- Broad circuit breakers.

## Portfolio placement

Wave 3 — adapter projections and runtime policy

Primary priority: Resiliency

## Dependencies

- [Establish end-to-end execution control and outcome semantics](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/871)
- [Build the versioned operator contract and doctor interface](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/877)

## Migration and release policy

Preserve current stdio and HTTP invocation syntax until coordinated cutover. New capacity settings must have safe documented defaults and additive configuration first.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Common lifecycle behavior has one implementation across stdio and HTTP.
- [ ] Capacity, expiry, and initialization limits are deterministic and recover after eviction.
- [ ] Disconnect and shutdown abort active Hevy work within the configured bound.
- [ ] Optional telemetry failure cannot block startup, requests, or cleanup.
- [ ] Existing raw-chunk stdio instrumentation and HTTP security tests remain green.

## Validation

- `npm run test:stdio`
- `npm run test:contract`
- `npm run test:worker-http`
- `npm run build`
- `npx vitest run --exclude tests/integration/**`
- `npm run check`
- `npm run check:types`
- `npm run check:changeset`

## Stopping conditions

- Do not introduce unbounded queues behind the admission limit.
- Stop if common lifecycle extraction erases real stdio/HTTP differences.

## Roadmap source

Portfolio decision: [Choose the improvement portfolio and breaking-change migration policy](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/866)

Architecture source: [Synthesize deep-module boundaries and cross-cutting opportunities](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/865#issuecomment-5166093667)

The key correction is to finish that design—especially the shallow operations module—rather than inventing a universal Node/Worker host that would erase real state and authentication differences.

Architecture review Snapshot 2443cad 7 August 2026 Read-only

One deep application spine.
Three honest runtime hosts.

The repository already has the right macro-shape. The best architecture is to deepen the runtime-neutral operation and capability modules, then keep Node stdio, Node HTTP, and the Cloudflare Worker as independent adapters with their own lifecycle, authentication, and state.

Top recommendation

Finish the shared operations kernel; do not add a universal runtime base class.

The first bounded slice should centralize endpoint policy, then continue operations domain by domain.

Decision in one minute

Preserve the seams that are real

  • Deep shared modules: Hevy client mechanics, endpoint/execution policy, domain operations, capability semantics, and MCP projection.
  • Concrete adapters: Node stdio, stateful Node HTTP, stateless Worker HTTP/OAuth, and CLI presentation.
  • Shared semantic events: safe tool, cache, request, and outcome observations; exporters remain runtime-specific.
  • No transport unification: stateful sessions and process shutdown are not the same problem as isolated Worker requests.
This report deliberately stops before concrete TypeScript interface design. Candidate selection comes first.

Recommended target shape

The architecture is asymmetrically deep

Core is already deep and valuable. Operations is still a pilot. Runtime observation is rich on Node and coarse on Worker. Those asymmetries, not the package diagram itself, are the main sources of change amplification.

01

Complete the operations and capability kernel

Strongest

Turn the one-operation pilot into the application module that owns Hevy intent and policy across MCP and CLI.

Files and evidence

  • packages/operations/src/index.ts:18-29 — only workouts.list.
  • packages/operations/src/workouts.ts:10-101 — the entire production implementation.
  • packages/core/src/tools/* — 13 direct client call sites versus one operations call.
  • packages/cli/src/commands/index.ts:97-448 — most orchestration still bypasses operations.
  • Existing owner: issue #872.

Problem

Expected absence, pagination, search, mutation semantics, and composite workflows still live in presentation modules. The operations module is too shallow to justify its seam under the deletion test.

Direction

Migrate vertical domains incrementally. Operations owns intent-level normalization and outcomes; core owns MCP schemas and response presentation; CLI owns parsing and rendering. Delete superseded policy and tests as each slice lands.

Before → after

flowchart TB
  subgraph B["Before"]
    BC["MCP core"] --> BCL["Hevy client"]
    BCLI["CLI"] --> BCL
    BOPS["operations\nworkouts.list only"] --> BCL
    BC -. one call .-> BOPS
  end
  subgraph A["After"]
    ACORE["MCP projection"] --> AOPS["Deep operations\n+ capability kernel"]
    ACLI["CLI adapter"] --> AOPS
    AOPS --> ACL["Hevy client"]
  end

  classDef after fill:#123047,stroke:#3dd6d0,color:#fff

  class ACORE,AOPS,ACLI,ACL after

Benefits

  • One policy owner for two real production adapters.
  • Core becomes a deeper MCP projection instead of a mixed application module.
  • Operation-level tests replace duplicated tool/CLI implementation tests.
  • Future runtime hosts reuse application behavior without new transport abstractions.
02

Create one endpoint-policy vocabulary

Best first slice

Centralize endpoint identity while keeping retry, absence, diagnostic safety, and metric identity as distinct facts.

Files and evidence

  • hevy-client-kubb.ts:137-186 — safe, expected-404, and dynamic endpoint lists.
  • core/utils/hevy-error-policy.ts:7-66 — overlapping read/list/mutation sets.
  • core/utils/error-policy.ts:99-149 — safe codes, endpoints, and source identities.
  • node/utils/hevy-client-observability.ts:19-45 — another endpoint normalizer.
  • Current routing owner: issue #937.

Problem

An endpoint change can drift among retry behavior, expected absence, privacy-safe diagnostics, operations behavior, and metric labels. A broad allowlist would be dangerous because those facts have different security and product meaning.

Direction

Give canonical endpoint identity one neutral owner and let each policy consume explicit facts. Unknown endpoints remain fail-closed. This is a bounded prerequisite for deepening operations and aligning observation.

Before → after

flowchart TB
  subgraph B["Before: repeated registries"]
    E1["client retry / expected 404"]
    E2["core absence policy"]
    E3["safe diagnostics"]
    E4["Node metric normalization"]
  end
  subgraph A["After: one identity, distinct facts"]
    ID["Canonical endpoint identity"] --> R["Retry facts"]
    ID --> N["Absence facts"]
    ID --> D["Diagnostic facts"]
    ID --> M["Metric identity"]
  end
  classDef before fill:#301d2a,stroke:#fb7185,color:#fff
  classDef after fill:#123047,stroke:#3dd6d0,color:#fff
  class E1,E2,E3,E4 before
  class ID,R,N,D,M after

Benefits

  • High change leverage with a small first migration.
  • Stronger privacy because unknown identity stays explicit.
  • Removes one major source of cross-module drift.
  • Creates stable vocabulary for operations and both observation adapters.
03

Deepen each runtime host without merging them

Strong

Improve locality inside Node and Worker while keeping three concrete transport lifetimes.

Files and evidence

  • node/src/index.ts:303-497 — duplicated stdio/HTTP lifecycle policy.
  • node/utils/streamable-http.ts:231-494 — stateful sessions, admission, disconnect, cleanup.
  • worker/src/worker.ts:323-566 — stateless exchange plus raw-key/OAuth routing.
  • worker/src/worker-oauth.ts:328-540 — OAuth grant and authorized request path.
  • Existing owners: #878 Node, #879 Worker, #876 protocol serving.

Problem

Node repeats startup, telemetry, failure classification, cancellation, and shutdown between stdio and HTTP. Worker normalizes origin/config more than once across raw-key and OAuth branches. A cross-runtime base class would hide rather than solve these differences.

Direction

Use one private Node lifecycle owner around two transport adapters. Use one Worker request-normalization owner before two auth adapters and one authenticated MCP exchange. Share only the primitive factory and neutral outcome vocabulary.

Recommended ownership

flowchart TB
  PF["Shared MCP primitive factory"] --> NL["Node lifecycle owner"]
  PF --> WR["Worker request owner"]
  NL --> S["stdio adapter"]
  NL --> H["stateful HTTP adapter"]
  WR --> A1["OAuth adapter"]
  WR --> A2["direct-key adapter\nself-hosted / transition"]
  A1 --> X["stateless authenticated exchange"]
  A2 --> X
  classDef shared fill:#123047,stroke:#3dd6d0,color:#fff
  classDef adapter fill:#2a2038,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
  class PF shared
  class NL,WR,S,H,A1,A2,X adapter

Guardrail

Do not make Node stateful sessions and Worker stateless requests implement one universal lifecycle. The official SDK and Cloudflare guidance explicitly support different deployment modes.

04

Close the Worker observation seam

Strong targeted move

Keep one safe semantic event vocabulary while projecting it through runtime-native sinks.

Files and evidence

  • core/src/observation.ts:53-127 — privacy-safe tool observation interface.
  • core/src/utils/cache.ts:10-32 — cache observation seam.
  • node/src/index.ts:264-277 — Node wires tool, cache, and client observers.
  • worker/src/worker.ts:220-244 — Worker passes only client logging.
  • cloudflare.config.ts:20-53 — platform observability is enabled.
  • Related owner: issue #928.

Problem

The Worker has request-level logs and platform traces, but no application-level tool, cache, retry, or Hevy-call correlation through the existing neutral interface. “No Worker observability” would be inaccurate; semantic parity is the gap.

Direction

Implement a Worker-native adapter over existing bounded observations. Keep Sentry and Node OTel packages out of the Worker graph. Exporters may differ; event meaning and privacy rules should not.

Before → after

flowchart LR
  subgraph B["Before"]
    EV1["safe core events"] --> NO["Node observer"]
    NO --> OT["OTel / Sentry"]
    WREQ["Worker request logs"] --> CF1["Cloudflare"]
  end
  subgraph A["After"]
    EV2["same safe events"] --> NO2["Node observer"]
    EV2 --> WO["Worker observer"]
    NO2 --> OT2["OTel / Sentry"]
    WO --> CF2["Cloudflare-native sink"]
  end
  classDef shared fill:#123047,stroke:#3dd6d0,color:#fff
  classDef adapter fill:#2a2038,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
  class EV1,EV2 shared
  class NO,OT,WREQ,CF1,NO2,WO,OT2,CF2 adapter

Benefits

  • Cross-runtime operational parity without exporter coupling.
  • One privacy review surface for semantic fields.
  • Tool and upstream failures become correlatable on Worker.
05

Separate Node embedding from executable startup

Worth exploring

Make the published programmatic interface safe to import without installing global telemetry providers.

Files and evidence

  • node/src/index.ts:1-37 — telemetry import must execute first.
  • node/utils/telemetry.ts:107-217 — import-time Sentry/OTel global setup.
  • node/src/index.ts:293-301 — public builder performs a network validation probe.
  • node/README.md:184-199 — published embedding contract.
  • node/tsdown.config.ts:58-99 — library and CLI share the same source graph.

Problem

The public library entrypoint and executable composition share import-time telemetry. An embedding application can therefore acquire global providers and network behavior merely by using the builder. This weakens locality and makes the interface shallower than its documentation suggests.

Direction

Separate a side-effect-free embedding entry from the executable bootstrap. The executable explicitly initializes telemetry, environment config, update checks, and process lifecycle before running the chosen transport.

Before → after

flowchart TB
  subgraph B["Before"]
    IMP["import hevy-mcp"] --> GLOBAL["global telemetry init"]
    GLOBAL --> BUILD["createNodeMcpServer"]
    GLOBAL --> RUN["run executable"]
  end
  subgraph A["After"]
    LIB["side-effect-free library entry"] --> BUILD2["embedded server composition"]
    EXE["executable entry"] --> INIT["telemetry + config + lifecycle"]
    INIT --> RUN2["stdio / HTTP runner"]
  end
  classDef before fill:#301d2a,stroke:#fb7185,color:#fff
  classDef after fill:#123047,stroke:#3dd6d0,color:#fff
  class IMP,GLOBAL,BUILD,RUN before
  class LIB,BUILD2,EXE,INIT,RUN2 after

Why not first?

This materially improves the public Node interface, but it does not resolve the larger shared-policy duplication. Coordinate it with Node lifecycle work rather than creating a second runner.

06

Prove the seam with one runtime contract matrix

Required proof

Exercise the same primitive catalog and outcome semantics through core, Node stdio, Node HTTP, and Worker HTTP.

Files and evidence

  • tests/integration/mocked/* — broad core contract coverage.
  • tests/integration/worker-http.integration.test.ts:504-705 — representative Worker coverage.
  • node/utils/streamable-http.test.ts — stateful host behavior.
  • worker/src/worker.test.ts:383-440 — fresh server/transport per Worker request.
  • Existing owner: issue #880.

Problem

Adapter tests prove local mechanics, but parity of every primitive, schema, safe outcome, and protocol era is not yet one generated contract. A seam with three runtime adapters needs interface-level proof.

Direction

Generate behavior cases from accepted capability descriptors, execute them through each supported host, and keep host-specific lifecycle tests separate. Tests consume the model; they do not redefine it.

Proof topology

flowchart LR
  MODEL["Capability + outcome model"] --> MATRIX["Generated contract matrix"]
  MATRIX --> CORE["in-memory core"]
  MATRIX --> STDIO["Node stdio"]
  MATRIX --> HTTP["Node HTTP"]
  MATRIX --> WORKER["Worker HTTP"]
  CORE --> REPORT["Parity report"]
  STDIO --> REPORT
  HTTP --> REPORT
  WORKER --> REPORT
  classDef shared fill:#123047,stroke:#3dd6d0,color:#fff
  classDef adapter fill:#2a2038,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
  class MODEL,MATRIX,REPORT shared
  class CORE,STDIO,HTTP,WORKER adapter

Benefits

  • Runtime parity becomes executable, not documentary.
  • Protocol upgrades expose drift before deployment.
  • Deep modules can replace shallow tests with confidence.

Recommended sequence

Small vertical moves toward the target

01

Endpoint identity

One identity owner; distinct fail-closed policy facts.

02

Operations domains

Migrate reads, writes, search, then workflows; delete duplicates.

03

MCP projection

Project capabilities through one primitive factory.

04

Runtime hosts

Refactor Node and Worker independently around their real lifetimes.

05

Parity proof

Conformance matrix plus runtime-native observation.

Decision record and current guidance

Repository decisions

  • #865 architecture synthesis
  • #866 accepted portfolio
  • #937 current-checkout review routing

Primary external guidance

  • MCP TypeScript SDK server guide — stateful/stateless deployment and host protection.
  • Cloudflare MCP handler guide — stateless Worker handler as the current default.

Method: current source inspection, deletion test, module depth, seam reality, change leverage, locality, adapter parity, live issue state, and current primary SDK/runtime guidance. No source or repository file was changed.

comments.body:
## Resolution

This decision was completed through live human grilling after [Synthesize deep-module boundaries and cross-cutting opportunities](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/865#issuecomment-5166093667).

## Portfolio decision

Accept synthesis candidates 1–8 and the evidence-driven contract/surface simplification portion of candidate 9.

Defer the MCP Apps prototype until the canonical capability model and evaluation harness demonstrate enough user value and supported-host coverage. Do not create an implementation issue for it in this portfolio.

### Breaking-change policy

- Deliver one coordinated major release rather than spreading public breaks across several majors.
- Build it through small, independently mergeable pull requests on `main`.
- Preparatory work must preserve current public behavior through additive fields, compatibility adapters, or internal-only movement.
- Remove approved aliases and incompatible behavior only in the explicit final cutover.
- Internal package/script/workflow composition may break earlier when no public contract changes and repository validation remains green.

### Authentication policy

- Hosted production uses the existing MCP OAuth flow.
- Remove only the hosted raw-Hevy-key-as-`Authorization: Bearer` fallback in the coordinated major.
- Preserve direct Hevy credentials for Node, CLI, Docker, and self-hosted Worker operation.
- Preserve Hevy’s upstream `api-key` header; it is unrelated to the MCP OAuth bearer-token boundary.

### Protocol policy

Keep 2025 and 2026 MCP support throughout the entire next major. The 2026 protocol is too new for a modern-only cutover. Removing 2025 support requires:

1. a later major release;
2. passing official conformance for the modern path;
3. evidence from supported clients/hosts; and
4. a separately reviewed migration and rollback plan.

### Evidence gate for public surface consolidation

A tool/resource removal or merge may proceed only when recorded evaluations show:

- no task-success regression;
- zero unsafe-mutation regression;
- at least 15% improvement in median call count or catalog token cost; and
- confirmation across at least two supported AI client/model families.

Missing the threshold defers the consolidation without blocking the major release.

## Five-wave implementation backlog

Every issue below is unassigned and includes an ownership seam, bounded scope, non-goals, linked dependencies, migration policy, acceptance criteria, validation commands, and stopping conditions.

### Wave 1 — correctness closure

- [Repair generated-client output closure and enforce regeneration drift](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/870) — fix the current Kubb destination defect and add hermetic regenerate-and-clean-diff enforcement.

### Wave 2 — deep foundations

- [Establish end-to-end execution control and outcome semantics](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/871) — cancellation, absolute deadlines, phase-aware failures, retry safety, ambiguous writes, and shared recovery semantics.
- [Create the shared Hevy operations and capability workspace](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/872) — move shared MCP/CLI operation policy behind a runtime-neutral deep module.
- [Centralize repository topology, artifact provenance, and validation lanes](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/873) — replace duplicated package, artifact, release, and lane registries with linked control-plane models.

### Wave 3 — adapter projections and runtime policy

- [Project MCP contracts from canonical capability descriptors](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/874) — structured mutation results, canonical fields, schema semantics, pagination, and MCP presentation metadata.
- [Deepen the CLI adapter and add safe mutation ergonomics](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/875) — domain-local commands, stable JSON errors, schema discovery, previews, confirmation, completion, and complete reads.
- [Serve dual-era MCP protocols through one primitive factory](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/876) — SDK-supported 2025/2026 serving without duplicate primitive definitions.
- [Build the versioned operator contract and doctor interface](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/877) — product/config/auth/readiness semantics and privacy-safe diagnostics.
- [Consolidate Node lifecycle and bound HTTP session capacity](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/878) — shared Node startup/shutdown plus deterministic admission and cleanup.
- [Normalize Worker routing and make OAuth the hosted-only production path](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/879) — one request-normalization path, outage-aware validation, OAuth default, and staged hosted-fallback removal.

### Wave 4 — proof and enforcement

- [Generate the complete MCP contract matrix and conformance lane](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/880) — generated coverage for every primitive and both protocol eras.
- [Build task-based AI-client evaluations and decision evidence](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/881) — deterministic intent scenarios, optional two-family matrix, safety/call/token metrics, and base/head reports.
- [Apply one validation model to CI, artifacts, coverage, and releases](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/882) — disjoint lanes, honest coverage, exact candidate gates, release simulations, health, and rollback.
- [Generate operator documentation, status, and recovery projections](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/883) — synchronized consumer, deployment, migration, recovery, and teardown facts.

### Wave 5 — evidence-gated simplification and coordinated major cutover

- [Rationalize MCP discovery surfaces only when evaluation gates pass](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/884) — implement only consolidations that satisfy the agreed evidence threshold; closing with no removals is valid when they do not.
- [Execute the coordinated major public-contract cutover](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/885) — remove approved aliases and the hosted raw-key fallback, publish synchronized major artifacts, retain 2025 MCP, and verify the actual release/deployment plus rollback.

## Dependency and concurrency decision

The immediately takeable implementation frontier is:

- [Repair generated-client output closure and enforce regeneration drift](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/870)
- [Establish end-to-end execution control and outcome semantics](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/871)
- [Centralize repository topology, artifact provenance, and validation lanes](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/873)

These three may proceed in parallel because they own separate seams. All later bodies link their prerequisites explicitly. The final cutover depends on the entire accepted portfolio; an evidence-based no-op resolution of surface rationalization still satisfies that dependency.

## Global implementation contract

Every implementation issue must:

- start from a fresh worktree tracking current `origin/main`;
- preserve runtime-neutral package boundaries and never manually edit generated client output;
- identify the single owner/model it introduces or extends and the duplicate owners it deletes;
- use small conventional commits and include the Changeset required by repository policy;
- retain current public behavior until the final cutover unless the issue is explicitly additive;
- prove behavior through the module interface and replace superseded shallow tests rather than layering duplicate tests;
- run build, unit, style, type, changeset, and issue-specific validation;
- distinguish deterministic candidate proof from live external canaries;
- state what remains unverified; and
- stop before weakening security, privacy, compatibility, or a required gate.

No delivery is considered complete until the actual package, container, Worker, or release event and its downstream state are verified end to end.

## Deferred and rejected work

Deferred:

- MCP Apps prototype, pending capability/evaluation foundations and host evidence.
- Removal of 2025 MCP support, pending a later major and ecosystem evidence.
- Performance timing thresholds, pending stable history and variance data.

Not advancing:

- broad circuit breakers without production evidence;
- indiscriminate stale user data or OAuth validity;
- merged Node/Worker transport implementations;
- Tasks, sampling, roots, legacy SSE, or form elicitation for credentials;
- universal progress notifications;
- a monolithic repository/product/capability manifest; and
- tool-count reduction without task evidence.

## Completion

The accepted portfolio is fully represented by linked implementation-ready issues, its dependency frontier is visible, compatibility and rollback policies are explicit, and no planning fog remains. No source, test, configuration, documentation, generated, or deployment file was changed while resolving this ticket.

payload.message: I’m taking the highest-ranked path forward: the shared operations/capability kernel. The architecture skill now moves from scanning into design, so I’m applying the “design it twice” check before settling the module seams and migration order.

The chosen seam must satisfy these constraints:

- It stays runtime-neutral: Web-standard cancellation/deadlines only; no Node process state, Cloudflare bindings, OAuth, Sentry, or OTel exporters.
- It serves two real production adapters—MCP and CLI—without becoming a generic string dispatcher or merely mirroring every generated Hevy client method.
- It owns Hevy intent: normalization, expected absence, pagination, search, composite workflows, mutation semantics, safety, and stable outcomes.
- MCP retains protocol schemas and presentation; CLI retains parsing, confirmation, and rendering; Node and Worker retain transport, authentication, lifecycle, and exporter implementations.
- The Hevy network is a true external dependency behind a local adapter; runtime observation is a local-substitutable port; clocks/signals are in-process controls.
- Adding a Hevy operation should change one domain module and its adapters, not a proxy index table, multiple endpoint lists, MCP logic, CLI logic, and several test harnesses.

A deliberately non-proposal sketch of the pressure on the seam is:

```ts
const operations = createHevyOperations({ hevy, observe });
const outcome = await operations.workouts.list(input, execution);
```

The design question is whether that shape should remain a small domain facade, become a descriptor-driven capability kernel, or expose a more extensible port-based model. I’m testing all three before recommending one.

name: codebase-design
description: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
---

# Codebase Design

Design **deep modules**: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam, testable through that interface. Use this language and these principles wherever code is being designed or restructured. The aim is leverage for callers, locality for maintainers, and testability for everyone.

## Glossary

Use these terms exactly — don't substitute "component," "service," "API," or "boundary." Consistent language is the whole point.

**Module** — anything with an interface and an implementation. Deliberately scale-agnostic: a function, class, package, or tier-spanning slice. _Avoid_: unit, component, service.

**Interface** — everything a caller must know to use the module correctly: the type signature, but also invariants, ordering constraints, error modes, required configuration, and performance characteristics. _Avoid_: API, signature (too narrow — they refer only to the type-level surface).

**Implementation** — what's inside a module, its body of code. Distinct from **Adapter**: a thing can be a small adapter with a large implementation (a Postgres repo) or a large adapter with a small implementation (an in-memory fake). Reach for "adapter" when the seam is the topic; "implementation" otherwise.

**Depth** — leverage at the interface: the amount of behaviour a caller (or test) can exercise per unit of interface they have to learn. A module is **deep** when a large amount of behaviour sits behind a small interface, **shallow** when the interface is nearly as complex as the implementation.

**Seam** _(Michael Feathers)_ — a place where you can alter behaviour without editing in that place; the *location* at which a module's interface lives. Where to put the seam is its own design decision, distinct from what goes behind it. _Avoid_: boundary (overloaded with DDD's bounded context).

**Adapter** — a concrete thing that satisfies an interface at a seam. Describes *role* (what slot it fills), not substance (what's inside).

**Leverage** — what callers get from depth: more capability per unit of interface they learn. One implementation pays back across N call sites and M tests.

**Locality** — what maintainers get from depth: change, bugs, knowledge, and verification concentrate in one place rather than spreading across callers. Fix once, fixed everywhere.

## Deep vs shallow

**Deep module** = small interface + lots of implementation:

```
┌─────────────────────┐
│   Small Interface   │  ← Few methods, simple params
├─────────────────────┤
│                     │
│  Deep Implementation│  ← Complex logic hidden
│                     │
└─────────────────────┘
```

**Shallow module** = large interface + little implementation (avoid):

```
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│       Large Interface           │  ← Many methods, complex params
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  Thin Implementation            │  ← Just passes through
└─────────────────────────────────┘
```

When designing an interface, ask:

- Can I reduce the number of methods?
- Can I simplify the parameters?
- Can I hide more complexity inside?

## Principles

- **Depth is a property of the interface, not the implementation.** A deep module can be internally composed of small, mockable, swappable parts — they just aren't part of the interface. A module can have **internal seams** (private to its implementation, used by its own tests) as well as the **external seam** at its interface.
- **The deletion test.** Imagine deleting the module. If complexity vanishes, it was a pass-through. If complexity reappears across N callers, it was earning its keep.
- **The interface is the test surface.** Callers and tests cross the same seam. If you want to test *past* the interface, the module is probably the wrong shape.
- **One adapter means a hypothetical seam. Two adapters means a real one.** Don't introduce a seam unless something actually varies across it.

## Designing for testability

Good interfaces make testing natural:

1. **Accept dependencies, don't create them.**

   ```typescript
   // Testable
   function processOrder(order, paymentGateway) {}

   // Hard to test
   function processOrder(order) {
     const gateway = new StripeGateway();
   }
   ```

2. **Return results, don't produce side effects.**

   ```typescript
   // Testable
   function calculateDiscount(cart): Discount {}

   // Hard to test
   function applyDiscount(cart): void {
     cart.total -= discount;
   }
   ```

3. **Small surface area.** Fewer methods = fewer tests needed. Fewer params = simpler test setup.

## Relationships

- A **Module** has exactly one **Interface** (the surface it presents to callers and tests).
- **Depth** is a property of a **Module**, measured against its **Interface**.
- A **Seam** is where a **Module**'s **Interface** lives.
- An **Adapter** sits at a **Seam** and satisfies the **Interface**.
- **Depth** produces **Leverage** for callers and **Locality** for maintainers.

## Rejected framings

- **Depth as ratio of implementation-lines to interface-lines** (Ousterhout): rewards padding the implementation. We use depth-as-leverage instead.
- **"Interface" as the TypeScript `interface` keyword or a class's public methods**: too narrow — interface here includes every fact a caller must know.
- **"Boundary"**: overloaded with DDD's bounded context. Say **seam** or **interface**.

## Going deeper

- **Deepening a cluster given its dependencies** — see [DEEPENING.md](DEEPENING.md): dependency categories, seam discipline, and replace-don't-layer testing.
- **Exploring alternative interfaces** — see [DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md](DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md): spin up parallel sub-agents to design the interface several radically different ways, then compare on depth, locality, and seam placement.
# Design It Twice

When the user wants to explore alternative interfaces for a chosen deepening candidate, use this parallel sub-agent pattern. Based on "Design It Twice" (Ousterhout) — your first idea is unlikely to be the best.

Uses the vocabulary in [SKILL.md](SKILL.md) — **module**, **interface**, **seam**, **adapter**, **leverage**.

## Process

### 1. Frame the problem space

Before spawning sub-agents, write a user-facing explanation of the problem space for the chosen candidate:

- The constraints any new interface would need to satisfy
- The dependencies it would rely on, and which category they fall into (see [DEEPENING.md](DEEPENING.md))
- A rough illustrative code sketch to ground the constraints — not a proposal, just a way to make the constraints concrete

Show this to the user, then immediately proceed to Step 2. The user reads and thinks while the sub-agents work in parallel.

### 2. Spawn sub-agents

Spawn 3+ sub-agents in parallel using the Agent tool. Each must produce a **radically different** interface for the deepened module.

Prompt each sub-agent with a separate technical brief (file paths, coupling details, dependency category from [DEEPENING.md](DEEPENING.md), what sits behind the seam). The brief is independent of the user-facing problem-space explanation in Step 1. Give each agent a different design constraint:

- Agent 1: "Minimize the interface — aim for 1–3 entry points max. Maximise leverage per entry point."
- Agent 2: "Maximise flexibility — support many use cases and extension."
- Agent 3: "Optimise for the most common caller — make the default case trivial."
- Agent 4 (if applicable): "Design around ports & adapters for cross-seam dependencies."

Include both [SKILL.md](SKILL.md) vocabulary and CONTEXT.md vocabulary in the brief so each sub-agent names things consistently with the architecture language and the project's domain language.

Each sub-agent outputs:

1. Interface (types, methods, params — plus invariants, ordering, error modes)
2. Usage example showing how callers use it
3. What the implementation hides behind the seam
4. Dependency strategy and adapters (see [DEEPENING.md](DEEPENING.md))
5. Trade-offs — where leverage is high, where it's thin

### 3. Present and compare

Present designs sequentially so the user can absorb each one, then compare them in prose. Contrast by **depth** (leverage at the interface), **locality** (where change concentrates), and **seam placement**.

After comparing, give your own recommendation: which design you think is strongest and why. If elements from different designs would combine well, propose a hybrid. Be opinionated — the user wants a strong read, not a menu.

# Deepening

How to deepen a cluster of shallow modules safely, given its dependencies. Assumes the vocabulary in [SKILL.md](SKILL.md) — **module**, **interface**, **seam**, **adapter**.

## Dependency categories

When assessing a candidate for deepening, classify its dependencies. The category determines how the deepened module is tested across its seam.

### 1. In-process

Pure computation, in-memory state, no I/O. Always deepenable — merge the modules and test through the new interface directly. No adapter needed.

### 2. Local-substitutable

Dependencies that have local test stand-ins (PGLite for Postgres, in-memory filesystem). Deepenable if the stand-in exists. The deepened module is tested with the stand-in running in the test suite. The seam is internal; no port at the module's external interface.

### 3. Remote but owned (Ports & Adapters)

Your own services across a network boundary (microservices, internal APIs). Define a **port** (interface) at the seam. The deep module owns the logic; the transport is injected as an **adapter**. Tests use an in-memory adapter. Production uses an HTTP/gRPC/queue adapter.

Recommendation shape: *"Define a port at the seam, implement an HTTP adapter for production and an in-memory adapter for testing, so the logic sits in one deep module even though it's deployed across a network."*

### 4. True external (Mock)

Third-party services (Stripe, Twilio, etc.) you don't control. The deepened module takes the external dependency as an injected port; tests provide a mock adapter.

## Seam discipline

- **One adapter means a hypothetical seam. Two adapters means a real one.** Don't introduce a port unless at least two adapters are justified (typically production + test). A single-adapter seam is just indirection.
- **Internal seams vs external seams.** A deep module can have internal seams (private to its implementation, used by its own tests) as well as the external seam at its interface. Don't expose internal seams through the interface just because tests use them.

## Testing strategy: replace, don't layer

- Old unit tests on shallow modules become waste once tests at the deepened module's interface exist — delete them.
- Write new tests at the deepened module's interface. The **interface is the test surface**.
- Tests assert on observable outcomes through the interface, not internal state.
- Tests should survive internal refactors — they describe behaviour, not implementation. If a test has to change when the implementation changes, it's testing past the interface.

issue.title: Project MCP contracts from canonical capability descriptors
issue.body:
## Outcome

All MCP tools, prompts, and resources project selection intent, schemas, outputs, safety, field mappings, and recovery semantics from the accepted capability model.

## Ownership seam

`@hevy-mcp/core` remains the MCP capability adapter. It owns MCP registration and presentation metadata but no longer owns duplicate Hevy orchestration or failure taxonomy.

## Scope

- Publish schema-validated structured results for every mutation while retaining text compatibility until cutover.
- Generate/validate concise field units, formats, omit/null behavior, replacement semantics, and examples.
- Adopt canonical `superset_id` internally and expose the legacy output alias until the major cutover.
- Make pagination defaults/integer rules and continuation evidence consistent in structured and text presentations.
- Project write safety, patch/replace/create semantics, titles, icons, completion metadata, and resource-link/cache-hint policy.
- Put guided workout safety on a universally callable path.

## Non-goals

- Reducing tool count without evaluation evidence.
- Implementing MCP Apps.
- Moving transport serving into core.
- Inventing completion data or weakening confirmation safeguards.

## Portfolio placement

Wave 3 — adapter projections and runtime policy

Primary priority: AI-client ergonomics

## Dependencies

- [Establish end-to-end execution control and outcome semantics](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/871)
- [Create the shared Hevy operations and capability workspace](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/872)

## Migration and release policy

Add new fields and structured results before cutover. Remove legacy field aliases or incompatible contract shapes only in the coordinated major. Include appropriate package Changesets.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every mutation advertises and validates a public success schema.
- [ ] Every capability has machine-verifiable safety and outcome semantics.
- [ ] Routine-to-workout composition requires no guessed field translation.
- [ ] All paginated presentations expose correct continuation/end-of-list evidence.
- [ ] Tools, prompts, resources, instructions, token measurement, and contract tests detect descriptor drift.

## Validation

- `npm run test:contract`
- `npm run test:mcp`
- `npm run measure:tokens -- --enforce-budget`
- `npm run build`
- `npx vitest run --exclude tests/integration/**`
- `npm run check`
- `npm run check:types`
- `npm run check:changeset`

## Stopping conditions

- Do not remove or merge a public capability in this issue.
- Stop if descriptor generation hides MCP-specific semantics instead of validating explicit adapter choices.

issue.title: Create the shared Hevy operations and capability workspace
issue.body:
## Outcome

MCP and CLI consume one runtime-neutral module for Hevy operation policy and typed capability descriptors instead of independently orchestrating the curated client.

## Ownership seam

A new `@hevy-mcp/operations` workspace owns intent-level reads/writes, normalization, expected absence, pagination, search, composite workflows, cache/degradation policy, mutation semantics, canonical field metadata, and capability identifiers.

## Scope

- Insert `hevy-client → operations → core → node/worker`, with `operations → cli`, while preserving runtime neutrality.
- Move shared orchestration out of MCP tools/workflows and CLI dispatch behind a small typed interface.
- Define canonical operation descriptors for intent, input/output, safety, field mappings, and outcome contract.
- Provide an in-memory Hevy adapter and test behavior through the operations interface.
- Delete superseded duplicated policy and tests once equivalent interface-level coverage exists.

## Non-goals

- A generic stringly operation dispatcher.
- Merging MCP schemas with generated Hevy schemas.
- Owning CLI rendering, MCP registration, transports, or runtime lifecycle.
- Exposing generated Kubb internals as public package API.

## Portfolio placement

Wave 2 — deep foundations

Primary priority: Maintainer leverage

## Dependencies

- [Establish end-to-end execution control and outcome semantics](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/871)

## Migration and release policy

Internal architecture may break private imports, but public MCP/CLI behavior must remain compatible until the coordinated major cutover. Add an empty Changeset when no runtime behavior changes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] MCP and CLI execute shared operations through the new interface.
- [ ] Pagination, absence, mutation replacement/patch rules, search, and composite workflows each have one implementation owner.
- [ ] The workspace passes package-boundary, export, bundle, and Changeset propagation checks.
- [ ] Interface-level tests replace duplicated implementation tests without reducing behavioral coverage.
- [ ] Deleting the module would demonstrably redistribute policy across both adapters.

## Validation

- `npm run check:workspaces`
- `npm run check:boundaries`
- `npm run check:exports`
- `npm run build:packages`
- `npx vitest run --exclude tests/integration/**`
- `npm run check`
- `npm run check:types`
- `npm run check:changeset`

## Stopping conditions

- Do not expose a broad interface mirroring every generated client method without hiding policy.
- Stop if Node built-ins or Worker-specific globals enter the runtime-neutral workspace.

## Roadmap source

Portfolio decision: [Choose the improvement portfolio and breaking-change migration policy](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/866)

Architecture source: [Synthesize deep-module boundaries and cross-cutting opportunities](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/865#issuecomment-5166093667)

issue.title: Establish end-to-end execution control and outcome semantics
issue.body:
## Outcome

Every MCP, CLI, Node, and Worker invocation carries one cancellation signal and absolute deadline to Hevy, and every completion or failure produces a stable, privacy-safe outcome with retry and commit-state semantics.

## Ownership seam

A runtime-neutral execution/outcome module owns caller control, operation safety, request phase, commit state, safe failure taxonomy, and recovery fields. Adapters own only presentation and protocol/status mapping.

## Scope

- Add request control to every curated Hevy client operation and make fetch, body reads, backoff, pagination, and composite work abortable.
- Track dispatch/response phases and distinguish `not_sent`, `confirmed`, and `unknown` mutation outcomes.
- Select retryability from declared operation safety and remaining deadline; honor usable `Retry-After` values with jitter.
- Project the same safe outcomes into MCP structured errors, CLI exit/JSON errors, HTTP responses, and telemetry.
- Feed disconnect, eviction, SIGINT, and shutdown cancellation into active work.

## Non-goals

- Broad circuit breakers.
- Automatic retry of non-idempotent writes.
- Adapter-specific prose inside the shared model.
- Serving stale sensitive user data.

## Portfolio placement

Wave 2 — deep foundations

Primary priority: Resiliency

## Dependencies

- None. This issue is an immediate start within its wave.

## Migration and release policy

issue.title: Synthesize deep-module boundaries and cross-cutting opportunities
issue.body:
## Question

Across the architecture, resilience, operator, AI-client, safety-net, and ecosystem audits, which findings are the same underlying problem, where should ownership and abstraction boundaries move, and what deduplicated set of evidence-backed opportunities should advance to portfolio selection?

## Wayfinder relationships

Parent map: [Chart a comprehensive hevy-mcp improvement roadmap](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/858)

Blocked by:

- [Map change-amplification and duplication hotspots](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/864)
- [Audit failure containment and recovery across runtimes](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/859)
- [Audit operator journeys from installation through diagnosis](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/861)
- [Audit MCP tool contracts for AI-client usability](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/862)
- [Audit test, generation, CI, and release safety nets](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/860)
- [Benchmark hevy-mcp against current MCP and SDK guidance](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/863)
